Each of the five selectable archetypes has five levels. Each level is a distinct environment along that archetype's continuous Progress journey in the Levels view: **five worlds, twenty-five environments**. This brief defines those places and develops Explorer's opening Dutch flower fields as the current art focus.

The user requested this complete environment brief. Explorer's five region identities are already implemented; their appearance is still under review. The other twenty environments and the detailed meadow composition below are proposed design directions, not claims of approved artwork or completed implementation. Environment names are working scene titles, not replacements for existing level or badge names.

This document owns the environment plan. [AVATAR_WORK_HANDOFF.md](AVATAR_WORK_HANDOFF.md) owns current implementation, latest user decisions, and device evidence. Its newest entries take precedence over historical experiments. Creating this brief does not place all twenty-five environments in the next release.

## Shared structure

- Each world has one continuous route through five places. Each environment contains its level's three badge blocks: 1–3, 4–6, 7–9, 10–12, and 13–15. Scenery supports those landmarks and the earned-position avatar piece.
- Preserve the five levels, 20 equal displayed steps per level, badge requirements, and 12,000-point total. The legacy seven-step model is retained only for older layouts. Region boundaries follow the existing level-to-route mapping. Do not divide the road into equal fifths or derive geographic position from raw total-points percentage.
- A new environment changes spatial form, dominant material, and recognizable landmarks together. A color swap alone is insufficient. Adjacent regions share an edge so movement feels continuous.
- Each level has an arrival, a defining middle, and an exit or final destination. These are composition beats around existing badges, not new tasks or rewards.
- Advancement means growing practice, range, and confidence. Later places need not become more expensive, prestigious, or crowded. The settings do not require the user to pursue a particular sport, art medium, career, or lifestyle.
- Preserve the four camera heights: Close, Medium, High, and Wide. Design spaces as open landscapes, courtyards, or roofless viewing areas; roofs and overhead structures must not conceal the route at higher views.
- Since 2026-10-08 Progress is gated to the user's reached level (final_revisions.md, Levels directive 1): scrolling stops before the reached level's last badge, the next level stays loaded and visible ahead as a glimpse, and nothing beyond it loads. Test and capture modes stay unrestricted for inspection. There are still no walls or doors; the planned boundary marker is a cloud bank (an exception to the no-clouds rule below, recorded when it is built). Transitions in this brief are visual changes, not locks.
- Keep the current neutral road, badge artwork, avatar piece, centered camera behavior, and heavy scrolling. The horizontal look gesture below is a separate camera change; scenery work alone must preserve camera behavior.

## Levels view: horizontal look gesture

On 2026-09-21, the user proposed a horizontal navigator for looking a little farther to either side of the narrow path. This belongs to the Levels view, with Explorer Level 1 as the first place to evaluate it. The user subsequently requested implementation. The gesture and a compact horizontal indicator are now implemented; see the handoff for physical-device verification status.

- Drag left or right to look slightly toward that side of the environment. The look amount follows the finger and stops at a modest limit. Holding the finger off-center holds the view there.
- Releasing the finger returns the view smoothly to the centered path framing. Cancelling the gesture or leaving the view also clears the temporary offset. There is no sideways inertia or saved off-center position.
- Horizontal looking preserves the current position along the route. Vertical dragging retains its existing forward/backward movement and weight. Distinguish the intended axis so small diagonal movements do not accidentally advance the journey while looking around.
- Keep all four camera heights usable. The centered pose remains the current authored pose; limit the sideways look so the route stays visible and nearby terrain or the windmill never clips through the camera.
- With Reduce Motion, keep direct finger control and return to center without spring overshoot or prolonged automatic motion.

The implementation uses direct touch on the scene and a small bottom-centered horizontal indicator. Dragging through 30% of the scene width reaches the limit of six degrees in either direction. The camera turns in place, preserving its authored position and terrain clearance. The first clear drag direction owns the gesture until release or cancellation. Return motion decays without overshoot using the existing camera frame clock; Reduce Motion recenters immediately. The offset is temporary and is cleared when leaving the view, changing archetypes, or backgrounding the app. Validate release and cancellation, axis separation, each camera height, and unchanged route position on the physical iPhone.

## The twenty-five environments

### Explorer — from an open beginning to a high mountain destination

The current alpine journey expresses curiosity through changing terrain and deeper observation. Keep the established sequence. Its final destination remains the accepted enclosing mountain valley at summit elevation; do not replace it with a lone peak or an exposed road into empty space.

| Level | Environment          | Spatial character and defining landmarks                                                                                                                                     | Meaning and transition                                                                                                       |
| ----- | -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1     | **Dutch Flower Fields**      | Dense Dutch-style tulip fields in broad red, pink, gold, ivory, and purple bands. An octagonal windmill stands among the beds, with a brown timber barn and small trimmed patch on the right of the route; the existing forest remains ahead. | Begin with curiosity and room to look around. Grass becomes rougher and scattered trees gather at the forest edge.           |
| 2     | **Forest Foothills** | Irregular pine stands on rising ground, open gaps between branches, moss and exposed earth, and a winding stream beside the route.                                           | Learn to notice and navigate. Trees thin around larger rock faces as the stream leads toward the valley.                     |
| 3     | **Mountain Valley**  | A recessed pool or lake, an irregular shoreline, a rock escarpment, and a visible waterfall framed by larger peaks.                                                          | Reach the first substantial discovery and pause to take it in. Water recedes behind the route as the ground becomes stonier. |
| 4     | **Exposed Ridge**    | An open crest with depressed flanks, weathered rock ribs, sparse grass, and longer views. Keep the route crest clear.                                                        | Develop confidence in more demanding terrain. Warm weathered stone gives way to cooler granite and the first snow patches.   |
| 5     | **Alpine Summit**    | Cool granite, patchy snow, and tall enclosing peaks around the final high valley. The final badge sits within a complete destination composition.                            | Arrival and perspective. The enclosing landform ends this journey without implying a sixth region.                           |

### Athlete — a connected landscape for movement and disciplined practice

Use a landscaped sports campus with increasingly defined spaces, rather than five copies of a gym. Rhythm, clear spans, and purposeful equipment establish identity. Different sports illustrate breadth; they are not level-specific obligations.

| Level | Environment         | Spatial character and defining landmarks                                                                                                                              | Meaning and transition                                                                                                                   |
| ----- | ------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1     | **Movement Garden** | An open lawn with a curved warm-up track beside the Progress road, a shaded training bench, and a simple stretching rail. Low hedges frame generous space.            | Establish the habit of showing up. The garden's curves straighten toward a more structured practice court.                               |
| 2     | **Training Court**  | A sunken, open-air court with rubber and pale stone surfaces, a sheltered equipment edge, and one recognizable apparatus such as parallel bars.                       | Repetition and technique. A long opening in the court reveals water and a lower waterside terrace.                                       |
| 3     | **Rowing Basin**    | A straight, calm training basin, a low boathouse silhouette, and a rowing shell on a rack. Water sits beside the route, never under an unsupported road.              | Sustain rhythm and endurance. The basin's long horizontal edge leads toward an athletics field.                                          |
| 4     | **Athletics Field** | An oval track, a clear infield, and a short ordered run of hurdles on a separate practice lane. Low seating defines the perimeter.                                    | Bring practiced skills together. The track's arc guides the eye toward the final arena entrance.                                         |
| 5     | **Open Arena**      | A compact stadium bowl with stepped seating, a broad central field, and a quiet laurel court at the endpoint. The Progress road remains distinct from sporting lanes. | Demonstrate capacity and recognize sustained work. The enclosing stands complete the world without podium rankings or an animated crowd. |

### Artist — from observation to making and sharing

Use a connected creative quarter. Include visual art, material craft, and music so the world does not imply that every Artist must become a painter. Architecture is warm and practical, with pigment used selectively.

| Level | Environment           | Spatial character and defining landmarks                                                                                                                     | Meaning and transition                                                                                                     |
| ----- | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1     | **Sketch Garden**     | A planted courtyard with an open drawing table, one easel, and an interesting stone form to observe. Broad paving and quiet walls give the objects room.     | Notice and begin making. The courtyard opens into a working studio terrace.                                                |
| 2     | **Working Atelier**   | Open studio bays with a tall window-wall silhouette, worktables, stacked canvases, and a paint trolley. Keep roofs away from the route.                      | Build a repeatable practice. Work surfaces and paving continue into a more material-focused workshop.                      |
| 3     | **Maker's Yard**      | A brick and clay workyard with a potter's wheel, drying shelves, and broad hanging print sheets. Objects look supported and usable.                          | Explore materials and refine technique. Brick gives way to an open performance court beyond the workshop.                  |
| 4     | **Rehearsal Court**   | An open bandstand beside a rehearsal terrace, with a piano beneath its shelter and shallow audience steps facing across the scene.                           | Develop expression through rehearsal and collaboration. The steps broaden into a garden for finished work.                 |
| 5     | **Exhibition Garden** | A sequence of outdoor gallery walls and sculptural plinths ending in a generous courtyard with one defining sculpture. Finished work is spaced deliberately. | Share a body of work and reflect on a personal voice. The final courtyard provides closure without implying fame or sales. |

### Culinarian — from ingredients to a shared table

Use one garden-and-market village connected by working courtyards. The journey expands from sourcing and preparation to feeding others. It should feel welcoming and lived in rather than like an increasingly expensive restaurant ladder.

| Level | Environment               | Spatial character and defining landmarks                                                                                                      | Meaning and transition                                                                                                |
| ----- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1     | **Kitchen Garden**        | Low herb beds, a few vegetable rows, a water trough, and a small harvest table. Earth paths meet warm stone beside the Progress road.         | Notice ingredients and begin caring for them. Garden rows lead to the nearby produce market.                          |
| 2     | **Market Square**         | An open square framed by a few produce stalls, stacked crates, and restrained fabric awnings. Leave a clear central passage.                  | Learn to choose and combine. Produce and paving carry through to a preparation courtyard.                             |
| 3     | **Preparation Courtyard** | An open kitchen with a long workbench, sink, utensil rail, and shaded pantry edge. Walls frame rather than enclose the camera.                | Turn ingredients into practiced technique. The hearth and chimney become visible beyond the work area.                |
| 4     | **Bakehouse Court**       | A masonry oven, flour-toned paving, a bread-cooling rack, and a bakery cart beside an open working apron. The oven is the primary silhouette. | Develop timing, patience, and consistency. Baskets and warm paving lead toward the serving garden.                    |
| 5     | **Shared Table Garden**   | A broad dining terrace with a long prepared communal table, a serving sideboard, and low garden walls or an arbor at its perimeter.           | Complete the journey through hospitality. The table is the destination; no diners or service simulation are required. |

### Mannequin — from daily preparation to a deliberate public presence

Use a coherent city fashion quarter: smaller courtyards open into streets, studios, and a final skyline terrace. Style includes grooming, personal expression, and garment construction. Growth is not tied to luxury purchases or one body type.

| Level | Environment            | Spatial character and defining landmarks                                                                                                                                                                    | Meaning and transition                                                                                                          |
| ----- | ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1     | **Dressing Courtyard** | A quiet residential courtyard with an open dressing alcove, a full-length mirror, a garment rail, and a compact grooming table. Pale plaster and fabric soften the edges.                                   | Establish daily care and intentional choices. A side opening reveals the neighboring atelier.                                   |
| 2     | **Tailoring Atelier**  | Open workshop frontage with a cutting table, sewing station, dress form, and broad fabric panels. Timber and woven materials dominate.                                                                      | Understand fit, construction, and proportion. Workshop fronts become a continuous public street.                                |
| 3     | **Fashion Promenade**  | An urban pedestrian street with varied shopfronts, display windows, an orderly rhythm of street trees, and taller buildings beyond.                                                                         | Experiment with presentation in everyday life. The street opens toward a photographic studio court.                             |
| 4     | **Editorial Court**    | An open studio courtyard with a freestanding backdrop, a few substantial light stands, and bold architectural shadow shapes. A city station or elevated rail may appear at the outer edge as later scenery. | Refine presence and composition. Building setbacks reveal a wider skyline terrace; no overhead rail crosses the badge corridor. |
| 5     | **Skyline Salon**      | A broad terrace framed by stepped city towers, a restrained presentation platform, and a sculptural screen behind the endpoint. The scene reads as a finished city destination.                             | Express a coherent personal style. The skyline closes the composition without applause, celebrity, or shopping mechanics.       |

## Explorer Level 1: the next build

### What we are creating

A dense Dutch-style flower field at the beginning of an expedition, guided by the user’s tulip-field and windmill references. The viewer should recognize a particular place: a shallow grassy hollow crossed by the existing road, a Dutch windmill within broad tulip beds, low shoulders, and a forest entrance ahead. It should feel colorful, densely planted, and gently alive, while keeping the route and badges readable.

The scene must read at Wide before close-range detail is added. Its identity comes from the shape of the land and the relationship between open grass, exposed stone, flowers, and the distant treeline. On 2026-09-21 the user narrowed work to Explorer Level 1 and requested a Dutch flower field, far greater density, a breeze every few seconds, and a windmill. This replaces the earlier scattered-wildflower and timber-lookout direction.

### Layout along the existing route

Left and right below are relative to forward travel along the road. Adapt placement to the established camera rail; preserve the visual roles rather than forcing a landmark outside the frame.

A low limestone shoulder sits outside the road on the left; the right opens into a wider meadow. Introduce closely planted tulip beds in broad red, pink, gold, ivory, and purple bands that approach the actual road edge. Reveal the Dutch windmill ahead, offset from the badge.                                                                                    | A welcoming meadow, recognizable without a title.                       |

This is a proposed composition, not a request to move badges or rebuild the shared road. The terrain work stays within Level 1 and its narrow transition into Level 2. Preserve Levels 2–5, especially the enclosing final valley.

### Materials, light, and detail

- Use muted meadow greens with warmer straw notes in drier patches. Avoid uniform lime green, a global green tint, and alternating face colors.
- Mix short and medium grass through an irregular verge that reaches the actual road edge, with a few taller patches farther out. The user rejected broad clean strips and large empty circles around badges as looking recently mown. Protect only the narrow road clearance and actual badge bases; reduce plant height near them instead of clearing the surrounding ground. Large tonal groups should carry the Wide view; individual blades should not become a glittering field of specks.
- Keep limestone pale and weathered, with cleaved planes, narrow worn edges, and a visibly embedded base. Keep stone secondary to the windmill, with a few embedded fragments rather than a boulder garden.
- Use densely planted tulips in red, pink, gold, ivory, and purple bands. Their cup-shaped heads and long leaves must read at Close; continuous color beds must read at Wide. Small height and spacing variations soften the planting pattern. Preserve narrow safety clearances around the actual road and badge bases.
- Use broad, soft daylight and readable shadows. Keep distant pines cooler and quieter than the foreground. Do not add clouds, fog curtains, or a day/night system. Exception (2026-10-08, final_revisions.md Levels directive 2): the one universal cloud bank at the boundary to the level the user has not reached (`ProgressCloudBank`). It is the only cloud in any level, and the only scenery not made with Meshy, because it is scene weather, not a prop: code-drawn, unlit, and parting when the level is reached.
- A gentle breeze passes through the Level 1 flowers and grass approximately every 4.5 seconds, with roots fixed and a traveling phase across the field. The windmill sails rotate slowly. Reduce Motion freezes both effects. Insects, birds, sound, and a weather system remain outside this slice. Preserve the existing animated stream and waterfall elsewhere, including their Reduce Motion behavior.

### Asset scope

Reuse the current terrain generator, meadow flower geometry, fractured stone construction, and detailed pine geometry. On 2026-09-21 the user rejected the procedural windmill as too primitive and requested Meshy AI. Use the generated Dutch gallery windmill with textured brick, overlapping timber shingles, inset windows, an open white gallery, a curved cap, and four lattice sails. Clean and separate the rotor, retain its true hub and existing animation, and include its full sweep in camera and badge-sightline checks. The terrain generator loads the prepared Meshy source through `tools/meshy/explorer_windmill_asset.py`; source preparation and evidence live in `Methods_Images/explorer-meshy-windmill/`.

The user has now requested a Dutch windmill; this supersedes both the original tower exclusion and the interim timber-lookout design. Add one windmill as scenery, without an interaction or new progression mechanic. Tents, lodges, canoes, bridges, floatplanes, and additional routes remain outside this meadow pass. The requested Meshy replacement used one reference-image and image-to-3D candidate, costing 24 Meshy credits. Further generations are not part of this replacement.

### Acceptance criteria for the meadow implementation

1. At Wide, the opening reads as a dense tulip field with a recognizable Dutch windmill, low stone shoulders, and a forest destination ahead. It remains distinguishable from Level 2 without relying on labels.
2. At Close and Medium, grass, stone, and flowers retain convincing scale, surface detail, and grounding. Stone does not look inflated; plants do not float or visibly intersect the road.
3. All three Level 1 badge faces, the earned arrow, and the route remain readable at all four camera heights. Terrain and props do not intersect the camera or obscure the controls.
4. The sequence has three distinct views: entry hollow, broad flowered meadow, and forest threshold. Repeated props do not form a uniform border along the road.
5. The existing Level 1/2 boundary remains aligned with its badge groups. Scroll through the transition in both directions without a hard terrain seam or sudden material jump.
6. Route geometry, badge placement, camera poses, scroll weight, saved account data, and the test modes' unrestricted access remain unchanged (outside them Progress is gated to the reached level since 2026-10-08). Levels 2–5 retain their current composition and water behavior.
7. Capture entry, middle, and forest threshold at Close, Medium, High, and Wide on the physical iPhone. Compare the opening before and after, inspect intermediate motion, and run the existing terrain/camera and account-preservation checks appropriate to the change.
8. With the camera stationary, verify that flowers sway through a complete gust cycle and sails rotate independently. Reduce Motion must freeze both. Breeze offsets and the entire sail sweep must preserve road and badge clearance.
9. Record measured performance scope accurately. Callback cadence is not proof of GPU frame pacing; do not call visual or thermal performance verified without relevant measurements.

The slice is ready for user aesthetic review when those checks pass and the twelve native composition views are available. Device checks do not constitute user aesthetic approval. If the phone is unavailable, stop at an iOS device compile check and record runtime and visual review as not run; never use a simulator.

## Production sequence and asset reuse

1. Refine only Explorer's opening meadow using the detailed brief above. Save generated images and device captures under `Methods_Images/` with descriptive filenames, and update the handoff with the final evidence.
2. Use the meadow review to settle scene scale, density, and material quality before extending that treatment through Explorer's other four established regions.
3. For each remaining archetype, create a simple full-route layout showing all five spatial identities before detailing its first environment. The tables above are the working proposals; do not silently treat them as user-approved art.
4. Reuse suitable existing candidates after checking shape, scale, materials, and phone readability. Athlete has a pavilion, bench, hurdles, rowing shell, and fountain; Artist has an easel, trolley, wheel, piano, bandstand, and sculpture; Culinarian has planters, stalls, crates, oven, cart, and tables; Mannequin has a dress form, rail, mirror, sewing table, pavilion, and trunk. The catalog's cleanup notes still apply.
5. Create missing geometry only when its environment needs it. Candidate ownership does not require placing every asset, and historical Explorer or Mannequin experiments are not automatically restored.

The immediate deliverable from this planning task is this complete brief. App implementation, new artwork, and device verification belong to the subsequent environment work. No additional progression system, asset service, or general-purpose world editor is required by this plan.
